entry.sum: For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(X,\mu)$ is the space of measurable functions with $\|f\|_p=(\int|f|^p\,d\mu)^{1/p}<\infty$, modulo equality almost everywhere; $L^\infty$ uses the essential supremum. Hölder's and Minkowski's inequalities make each $L^p$ a normed space, the Riesz–Fischer theorem makes it complete, and $L^2$ is a Hilbert space. The exponent $p$ trades off penalising tall spikes (large $p$) against penalising slow decay (small $p$).
entry.why: They are the standard complete function spaces of analysis: Fourier analysis lives in $L^2$, PDE estimates and Sobolev spaces are built on $L^p$, and in probability $L^p$ norms are moments and $L^2$ is the space of finite-variance random variables.

links.note: Moments are $L^p$ norms of random variables, $L^2$ convergence is mean-square convergence, and Hölder and Jensen-type inequalities on a probability space bound expectations of products.
Plancherel makes the Fourier transform an isometry of $L^2$, and interpolation between $L^1$ and $L^2$ gives the Hausdorff–Young inequality for $1\le p\le 2$.
Weak solutions and energy estimates are formulated in Sobolev spaces, whose norms are $L^p$ norms of a function and its derivatives.

Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations

blocks.body:
How big is a function? The largest value it takes is one answer; the area under $|f|$ is another; the energy $\int|f|^2$, which appears in physics and in Fourier analysis, is a third. Each choice turns a space of functions into a [[normed-spaces|normed space]], and the family of choices $\big(\int|f|^p\big)^{1/p}$, indexed by $1 \le p \le \infty$, gives the $L^p$ spaces.

They are complete, which the Riemann-integrable functions are not; $L^2$ is a Hilbert space, the natural home of Fourier series and quantum mechanics; and the inequalities of Hölder and Minkowski that hold in them are the basic tools for estimating integrals in PDE, harmonic analysis and probability. This page assumes the [[lebesgue|Lebesgue integral]] on a measure space.

blocks.title: First impressions: the p-norms
blocks.body:
Start with vectors. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put $\|x\|_p = \big(\sum|x_i|^p\big)^{1/p}$ and $\|x\|_\infty = \max|x_i|$. For $x = (3,4)$:

$$\|x\|_1 = 7,\quad \|x\|_2 = 5,\quad \|x\|_3 = 91^{1/3} \approx 4.498,\quad \|x\|_\infty = 4.$$

The norms decrease in $p$ and tend to the largest coordinate. In the plane the unit ball $\{\|x\|_p \le 1\}$ is a diamond for $p = 1$, a disc for $p = 2$, and a square for $p = \infty$, with rounded squares in between.

For functions, $p$ decides which kind of bad behaviour is penalised. On $(0,1]$, the function $x^{-a}$ (with $a > 0$) has $\int_0^1 x^{-ap}\,dx < \infty$ exactly when $ap < 1$: large $p$ punishes tall spikes. On $[1,\infty)$, $\int_1^\infty x^{-ap}\,dx < \infty$ exactly when $ap > 1$: small $p$ punishes slow decay. So on a finite interval, $L^p$ shrinks as $p$ grows; on $\mathbb{R}$ neither space contains the other.

blocks.title: Lᵖ spaces
blocks.body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{M}, \mu)$ be a measure space and $1 \le p < \infty$. For measurable $f : X \to \mathbb{C}$ set

$$\|f\|_p = \Big(\int_X |f|^p\,d\mu\Big)^{1/p}, \qquad \|f\|_\infty = \inf\{M \ge 0 : |f| \le M \ \mu\text{-almost everywhere}\}$$

(the essential supremum). For $1 \le p \le \infty$, $L^p(X,\mu)$ is the set of measurable $f$ with $\|f\|_p < \infty$, where two functions are identified if they agree $\mu$-almost everywhere. For counting measure on $\mathbb{N}$ one writes $\ell^p$.

The identification is not pedantry: $\|f\|_p = 0$ means only that $f = 0$ almost everywhere, so without it $\|\cdot\|_p$ would not be a norm. Elements of $L^p$ are equivalence classes; their values at individual points are not defined.

blocks.title: Hölder's inequality
blocks.body:
Let $1 < p < \infty$ and let $q$ be the conjugate exponent, $\frac1p + \frac1q = 1$ (also $p = 1$, $q = \infty$). For measurable $f, g$,

$$\int_X |fg|\,d\mu \le \|f\|_p\,\|g\|_q.$$

For $1 < p < \infty$ and $\|f\|_p, \|g\|_q$ finite and non-zero, equality holds if and only if $|f|^p$ and $|g|^q$ are proportional almost everywhere. The case $p = q = 2$ is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

First Young's inequality: for $a, b \ge 0$, $ab \le \frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q}$, with equality iff $a^p = b^q$. If $a$ or $b$ is $0$ this is clear. Otherwise, since $\log$ is strictly concave ([[convexity]]),

$$\log\Big(\frac{a^p}{p} + \frac{b^q}{q}\Big) \ge \frac1p\log a^p + \frac1q\log b^q = \log(ab),$$

with equality iff $a^p = b^q$.

The case $p = 1$, $q = \infty$ is immediate from $|fg| \le |f|\,\|g\|_\infty$ a.e. For $1 < p < \infty$: if $\|f\|_p = 0$ or $\|g\|_q = 0$ then $fg = 0$ a.e. and both sides vanish; if either is infinite there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, by homogeneity we may scale so that $\|f\|_p = \|g\|_q = 1$. Apply Young pointwise with $a = |f(x)|$, $b = |g(x)|$ and integrate:

$$\int|fg|\,d\mu \le \frac1p\int|f|^p\,d\mu + \frac1q\int|g|^q\,d\mu = \frac1p + \frac1q = 1 = \|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$

Equality forces equality in Young almost everywhere, i.e. $|f|^p = |g|^q$ a.e. (after the scaling), which is the stated condition.

blocks.title: Minkowski's inequality
blocks.body: For $1 \le p \le \infty$ and $f, g \in L^p$, $\|f + g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$. Consequently $\|\cdot\|_p$ is a norm on $L^p$.

The cases $p = 1$ and $p = \infty$ follow from $|f + g| \le |f| + |g|$. Let $1 < p < \infty$. First, $L^p$ is closed under addition, since $|f + g|^p \le (2\max(|f|,|g|))^p \le 2^p(|f|^p + |g|^p)$. Now write $|f + g|^p \le |f|\,|f+g|^{p-1} + |g|\,|f+g|^{p-1}$ and apply Hölder to each term with exponents $p$ and $q = p/(p-1)$, noting $\big\||f+g|^{p-1}\big\|_q = \|f+g\|_p^{p-1}$:

$$\|f+g\|_p^p \le \big(\|f\|_p + \|g\|_p\big)\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}.$$

If $\|f + g\|_p = 0$ there is nothing to prove; otherwise divide by $\|f+g\|_p^{p-1}$.

blocks.title: Riesz–Fischer theorem
blocks.body: For every measure space and every $1 \le p \le \infty$, $L^p(X,\mu)$ is complete, hence a Banach space. Moreover, if $f_n \to f$ in $L^p$ with $p < \infty$, some subsequence converges to $f$ almost everywhere.

We treat $p < \infty$ (the case $p = \infty$ is a uniform-convergence argument off a null set). A normed space is complete if every absolutely convergent series converges: given a Cauchy sequence, choose $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ with $\|f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k}\| < 2^{-k}$; the telescoping series $f_{n_1} + \sum_k (f_{n_{k+1}} - f_{n_k})$ is absolutely convergent, its sum is the limit of the subsequence, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.

So let $g_k \in L^p$ with $\sum_k\|g_k\|_p = S < \infty$. Put $G_n = \sum_{k \le n}|g_k|$ and $G = \sum_k|g_k|$ (with values in $[0,\infty]$). By Minkowski, $\|G_n\|_p \le S$, and by monotone convergence $\int G^p = \lim\int G_n^p \le S^p$. So $G < \infty$ a.e., and on that set the series $\sum g_k(x)$ converges absolutely, to $F(x)$ say. Since $|F| \le G$, $F \in L^p$. Finally $|F - \sum_{k \le n}g_k|^p \le (2G)^p$, which is integrable, and the left side tends to $0$ a.e., so by dominated convergence $\|F - \sum_{k\le n}g_k\|_p \to 0$.

The a.e. statement comes out of the same argument: the subsequence $f_{n_k}$ chosen above converges a.e. to the limit, since the telescoping series converges absolutely a.e.

blocks.title: L² is special; how the spaces compare
blocks.body:
Only one of these spaces carries an inner product compatible with its norm. $L^2$ has $\langle f, g\rangle = \int f\bar g\,d\mu$ with $\langle f,f\rangle = \|f\|_2^2$, so with Riesz–Fischer it is a [[hilbert-spaces|Hilbert space]], with orthogonal projections and orthonormal bases. For $p \ne 2$ the parallelogram law $\|f+g\|^2 + \|f-g\|^2 = 2\|f\|^2 + 2\|g\|^2$ fails (see the example below), so no inner product induces $\|\cdot\|_p$.

How the spaces sit together:

- If $\mu(X) < \infty$ and $p < q$, then $L^q \subseteq L^p$ with $\|f\|_p \le \mu(X)^{1/p - 1/q}\|f\|_q$ (apply Hölder to $|f|^p \cdot 1$ with exponents $q/p$ and its conjugate).
- For sequences the inclusion goes the other way: $\ell^p \subseteq \ell^q$ for $p < q$, with $\|x\|_q \le \|x\|_p$.
- In general, if $p < q < r$ and $\frac1q = \frac\theta p + \frac{1-\theta}{r}$, then $\|f\|_q \le \|f\|_p^{\theta}\|f\|_r^{1-\theta}$. So $L^p \cap L^r \subseteq L^q$, and $\log\|f\|_{q}$ is a convex function of $1/q$.
- If $\mu(X) < \infty$ then $\|f\|_p \to \|f\|_\infty$ as $p \to \infty$.

blocks.title: Density, duality, and beyond
blocks.body: For readers continuing to functional analysis. Simple functions are dense in $L^p$ for every $p$ (integrable simple functions when $p < \infty$), and for $p < \infty$ the continuous functions with compact support are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This last fact fails for $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$, which is not even separable. For $1 \le p < \infty$ (and $\sigma$-finite $\mu$ when $p = 1$), every bounded linear functional on $L^p$ has the form $f \mapsto \int fg\,d\mu$ for a unique $g \in L^q$, so the dual of $L^p$ is $L^q$; for $1 < p < \infty$ this makes $L^p$ reflexive, whereas $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ are not (apart from finite-dimensional cases). Hölder's inequality and its equality case give $\|f\|_p = \sup\{|\int fg| : \|g\|_q \le 1\}$ for $1 \le p < \infty$, which together with [[hahn-banach]] is how many estimates are proved. The Riesz–Thorin theorem interpolates bounds for linear operators between $L^p$ spaces, giving for instance the Hausdorff–Young inequality for the [[fourier-transform]], and Sobolev spaces, built from functions whose derivatives lie in $L^p$, are the setting for the modern theory of PDE.

blocks.title: Which p? Spikes versus tails
blocks.body: (a) For which $p \in [1,\infty]$ is $f(x) = x^{-1/3}$ in $L^p(0,1)$? Compute $\|f\|_p$ when it is finite. (b) For which $p$ is $g(x) = x^{-1/3}$ in $L^p(1,\infty)$? (c) Find a function on $(0,\infty)$ that lies in $L^p$ for exactly one $p$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $\int_0^1 x^{-p/3}\,dx$ is finite iff $p/3 < 1$, i.e. $p < 3$, and then equals $\frac{1}{1 - p/3} = \frac{3}{3-p}$, so $\|f\|_p = \big(\frac{3}{3-p}\big)^{1/p}$. For instance $\|f\|_1 = 3/2$ and $\|f\|_2 = \sqrt3$. $f$ is unbounded, so $f \notin L^\infty$. Answer: $1 \le p < 3$.

(b) $\int_1^\infty x^{-p/3}\,dx < \infty$ iff $p > 3$; also $g \le 1$, so $g \in L^\infty$. Answer: $3 < p \le \infty$.

(c) Glue the two behaviours at the borderline: take $h(x) = x^{-1/2}\big(1 + |\ln x|\big)^{-1}$. Substituting $x = e^{u}$ turns $\int_0^\infty |h|^p\,dx$ into $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{u(1 - p/2)}(1+|u|)^{-p}\,du$. If $p \ne 2$ the exponential factor blows up at one end, so the integral diverges; if $p = 2$ it is $2\int_0^\infty (1+u)^{-2}\,du = 2$. So $h \in L^p(0,\infty)$ exactly for $p = 2$ (and $h \notin L^\infty$ since it blows up at $0$).

blocks.title: Hölder with the equality case
blocks.body: Find the largest possible value of $\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx$ over measurable $f \ge 0$ with $\int_0^1 f^3\,dx = 1$, and a function attaining it.
blocks.solution:
Hölder with $p = 3$ and $q = 3/2$ gives

$$\int_0^1 x f(x)\,dx \le \|f\|_3\,\|x\|_{3/2} = 1\cdot\Big(\int_0^1 x^{3/2}\,dx\Big)^{2/3} = \Big(\frac25\Big)^{2/3} \approx 0.5429.$$

Equality requires $f^3$ proportional to $x^{3/2}$, i.e. $f = c\sqrt x$. The constraint $\int_0^1 c^3x^{3/2}\,dx = \frac{2c^3}{5} = 1$ gives $c = (5/2)^{1/3}$. Check: $\int_0^1 x\cdot c\sqrt x\,dx = \frac{2c}{5} = \frac25\Big(\frac52\Big)^{1/3} = \Big(\frac25\Big)^{2/3}$. So the maximum is $(2/5)^{2/3}$.

blocks.title: Two structural facts
blocks.body: (a) Show that the parallelogram law fails in $L^p[0,1]$ for every $p \ne 2$. (b) Show that $\|f\|_p \to \|f\|_\infty$ as $p \to \infty$ when $\mu(X) < \infty$, and check it for $f(x) = x$ on $[0,1]$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Let $f = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1/2]}$ and $g = \mathbf{1}_{(1/2,1]}$. Then $|f + g| = |f - g| = 1$, so $\|f+g\|_p^2 + \|f-g\|_p^2 = 2$, while $2\|f\|_p^2 + 2\|g\|_p^2 = 4\cdot 2^{-2/p}$. These are equal iff $2^{-2/p} = 1/2$, i.e. $p = 2$. (For $p = \infty$ the right side is $4$.)

(b) Let $M = \|f\|_\infty$. For any $p$, $\|f\|_p \le M\mu(X)^{1/p} \to M$, so $\limsup\|f\|_p \le M$. For $\varepsilon \in (0, M)$, the set $A = \{|f| > M - \varepsilon\}$ has positive measure by definition of the essential supremum, and $\|f\|_p \ge (M - \varepsilon)\mu(A)^{1/p} \to M - \varepsilon$. So $\liminf\|f\|_p \ge M - \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$. (If $M = \infty$, the second argument with any finite level shows $\|f\|_p \to \infty$.)

For $f(x) = x$: $\|f\|_p = (p+1)^{-1/p}$, which is $1/2$ at $p = 1$, $1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.577$ at $p = 2$, about $0.955$ at $p = 100$, and tends to $1 = \|f\|_\infty$.

blocks.title: A three-term Hölder inequality
blocks.body:
Prove that for positive reals $a_i, b_i, c_i$ ($i = 1, \dots, n$),

$$\Big(\sum_i a_ib_ic_i\Big)^3 \le \Big(\sum_i a_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum_i b_i^3\Big)\Big(\sum_i c_i^3\Big).$$
blocks.solution:
Apply Hölder on $\ell^p$ with $p = 3$, $q = 3/2$ to the sequences $(a_i)$ and $(b_ic_i)$:

$$\sum a_ib_ic_i \le \Big(\sum a_i^3\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum (b_ic_i)^{3/2}\Big)^{2/3}.$$

Apply Cauchy–Schwarz ($p = q = 2$) to $(b_i^{3/2})$ and $(c_i^{3/2})$: $\sum (b_ic_i)^{3/2} \le \big(\sum b_i^3\big)^{1/2}\big(\sum c_i^3\big)^{1/2}$. Substituting,

$$\sum a_ib_ic_i \le \Big(\sum a_i^3\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum b_i^3\Big)^{1/3}\Big(\sum c_i^3\Big)^{1/3},$$

and cubing gives the claim. The same argument proves $\int|f_1\cdots f_k| \le \prod\|f_j\|_{p_j}$ whenever $\sum 1/p_j = 1$.

blocks.body:
- Convergence in $L^p$ does not imply convergence almost everywhere. The typewriter sequence (indicators of $[0,1],[0,\tfrac12],[\tfrac12,1],[0,\tfrac13],[\tfrac13,\tfrac23],\ldots$) tends to $0$ in every $L^p$ with $p < \infty$, yet at every point it takes the value $1$ infinitely often. Only a subsequence converges a.e.
- Conversely, a.e. convergence does not imply $L^p$ convergence: $n\mathbf{1}_{(0,1/n)} \to 0$ everywhere on $(0,1)$ but has $L^1$ norm $1$. Dominated convergence is the usual bridge.
- For $0 < p < 1$ the formula $(\int|f|^p)^{1/p}$ is not a norm: with $f = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1/2]}$, $g = \mathbf{1}_{(1/2,1]}$ and $p = 1/2$, $\|f+g\| = 1$ but $\|f\| + \|g\| = 1/2$.
- Inclusions depend on the measure: $L^2 \subseteq L^1$ on $[0,1]$ but not on $\mathbb{R}$ (take $1/(1+|x|)$), and $\ell^1 \subseteq \ell^2$ for sequences.
- $L^\infty$ is the essential supremum: changing $f$ on a null set does not change it, and $\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ has $\|\cdot\|_\infty = 0$ on $\mathbb{R}$.

$L^p$ spaces are the main examples of [[normed-spaces|Banach spaces]], and $L^2$ is the model [[hilbert-spaces|Hilbert space]]: [[fourier-series]] converge in $L^2$ by Parseval, and the [[fourier-transform]] is an isometry of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (Plancherel). Duality $(L^p)^* = L^q$ is a central application of the Radon–Nikodym theorem; integral operators with square-integrable kernels on $L^2$ are [[compact-operators]]. In probability, $L^p$ norms of [[random-variables]] are moments, $L^2$ convergence is mean-square convergence, and bounded families in $L^p$ ($p > 1$) are the uniformly integrable ones that [[martingales]] theory needs. Existence theory in the [[calculus-of-variations]] is set in Sobolev spaces built on $L^p$.

1. Show that if $\mu(X) = 1$ then $\|f\|_1 \le \|f\|_2 \le \|f\|_\infty$, and give an example on $[0,1]$ where both inequalities are strict.
2. Prove that $\ell^1 \subseteq \ell^2$ with $\|x\|_2 \le \|x\|_1$, and show that the inclusion is strict.
3. Let $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R}) \cap L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$. Prove that $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R})$ for every $1 \le p \le \infty$ and that $\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_1^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty^{1 - 1/p}$.
4. Prove that $L^\infty[0,1]$ is not separable by exhibiting uncountably many functions at pairwise distance $1$.

entry.sum: An entire function is holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$; its growth rate governs its structure, from Liouville's theorem (bounded implies constant) to the order of growth. Like a polynomial, an entire function can be written as a product over its zeros, but with convergence factors and an extra zero-free factor $e^{g(z)}$; for finite order, Hadamard's theorem makes $g$ a polynomial, as in Euler's $\sin\pi z = \pi z\prod(1 - z^2/n^2)$.
key: |f(z)|\le C(1+|z|)^N \;\Longrightarrow\; f \text{ is a polynomial of degree} \le N
f(z) = e^{P(z)}\, z^m \prod_{n} E_k(z/a_n),\quad \rho<\infty,\ k=\lfloor \rho\rfloor,\ \deg P\le k
entry.why: Product formulas evaluate series such as $\sum 1/n^2=\pi^2/6$, give the reflection formula for the Gamma function, and, through Hadamard's product for the completed zeta function, connect the zeros of $\zeta$ to the distribution of primes.

links.note: Hadamard's product for the completed Riemann zeta function over its nontrivial zeros underlies the explicit formula and the classical proof of the prime number theorem.
The Weierstrass product $1/\Gamma(z)=ze^{\gamma z}\prod(1+z/n)e^{-z/n}$ and the sine product together give the reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin\pi z$.

refs: Conway, Functions of One Complex Variable I

blocks.body:
A polynomial is determined, up to a constant factor, by its roots: $p(z) = c\prod(z - a_k)$. Entire functions, those holomorphic on the whole complex plane, are the natural infinite-degree analogue of polynomials. Can they, too, be built from their zeros? Euler treated $\sin \pi z$ as a polynomial with roots at the integers and wrote

$$\sin \pi z = \pi z\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}\Big(1 - \frac{z^2}{n^2}\Big),$$

from which he read off $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$. This page makes such formulas rigorous. The answer involves two new ingredients: convergence of infinite products, and a zero-free factor $e^{g(z)}$ that a polynomial does not need. How fast an entire function grows controls how simple both ingredients can be, which is the content of Hadamard's theorem, a key tool in the study of the Riemann zeta function.

blocks.title: Examples, and growth controls everything
blocks.body:
Polynomials, $e^z$, $\sin z$, $\cos z$, $e^{z^2}$ and $\cos\sqrt z = \sum_{n\ge0}(-1)^nz^n/(2n)!$ are entire. Their behaviour at infinity is very different from that of polynomials. $e^z$ has no zeros at all, so it cannot be a product over its zeros in the naive sense; $\sin z$ has infinitely many.

The first fact about entire functions comes straight from [[holomorphic|Cauchy's integral formula]]. If $f(z) = \sum a_nz^n$ is entire and $M(R) = \max_{|z| = R}|f(z)|$, the Cauchy estimates give

$$|a_n| \le \frac{M(R)}{R^n} \qquad \text{for every } R > 0.$$

So growth controls the Taylor coefficients, and through them the whole function.

blocks.title: Liouville's theorem, polynomial-growth form
blocks.body: Let $f$ be entire, and suppose $|f(z)| \le C(1 + |z|)^N$ for all $z$, for some constants $C$ and $N \ge 0$. Then $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N$. In particular (the case $N = 0$, Liouville's theorem), a bounded entire function is constant.

For $n > N$ and $R \ge 1$, the Cauchy estimate gives $|a_n| \le C(1+R)^N/R^n \le C\,2^NR^{N-n}$. Letting $R \to \infty$ gives $a_n = 0$. So the Taylor series, which converges to $f$ everywhere, has only the terms with $n \le N$.

blocks.title: Order of an entire function
blocks.body:
An entire function $f$ has order of growth $\rho_f$ if

$$\rho_f = \inf\big\{\rho \ge 0 : |f(z)| \le Ae^{B|z|^\rho} \text{ for all } z, \text{ for some constants } A, B > 0\big\}.$$

If no such $\rho$ exists the order is infinite. Order measures growth on an exponential scale: non-constant polynomials have order $0$; $e^z$, $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ have order $1$; $\cos\sqrt z$ has order $1/2$; $e^{z^2}$ has order $2$; $e^{e^z}$ has infinite order.

blocks.title: Infinite products
blocks.body:
An infinite product $\prod_{n\ge1}(1 + a_n)$ is said to converge if the partial products tend to a limit; the cleanest criterion is: if $\sum|a_n| < \infty$ then the product converges, and its value is $0$ only if some factor is $0$. The reason is the logarithm. For $|w| \le 1/2$, the principal logarithm satisfies $|\log(1 + w)| \le 2|w|$, so if all $|a_n| \le 1/2$ (true for all but finitely many $n$),

$$\prod_{n\le N}(1 + a_n) = \exp\Big(\sum_{n\le N}\log(1 + a_n)\Big),$$

and the series in the exponent converges absolutely. Its limit $L$ gives the product's value $e^L \ne 0$.

The same estimate, made uniform, gives the version for functions: if $F_n$ are holomorphic on an open set $\Omega$ and $\sum|F_n(z)|$ converges uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$, then $\prod(1 + F_n(z))$ converges uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function $F$ (a uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic), whose zeros are exactly the zeros of the factors. Where $F \ne 0$, differentiating term by term gives the logarithmic derivative

$$\frac{F'}{F} = \sum_n\frac{F_n'}{1 + F_n}.$$

For the sine product, $F_n(z) = -z^2/n^2$ and $\sum|z|^2/n^2$ converges uniformly on bounded sets. The product $\prod(1 - z/n)$, by contrast, does not converge for $z \ne 0$, because $\sum 1/n$ diverges; pairing $n$ with $-n$, or inserting factors $e^{z/n}$, rescues it.

blocks.title: Product formula for the sine
blocks.body:
For every $z \in \mathbb{C}$,

$$\sin\pi z = \pi z\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}\Big(1 - \frac{z^2}{n^2}\Big),\qquad\text{and}\qquad \pi\cot\pi z = \frac1z + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2z}{z^2 - n^2}\quad (z \notin \mathbb{Z}).$$

Step 1: the cotangent series, by [[residues]]. Fix $z \notin \mathbb{Z}$ and let $C_N$ be the boundary of the square with vertices $(N + \tfrac12)(\pm1 \pm i)$, for $N > |z|$. On the vertical sides $\cot\pi w = -i\tanh(\pi\operatorname{Im}w)$, of modulus at most $1$; on the horizontal sides $$|\cot\pi w| \le \coth\big(\pi(N + \tfrac12)\big) \le \coth(\pi/2) < 2$$. So $|\cot\pi w| \le 2$ on every $C_N$.

Consider $k(w) = \pi\cot(\pi w)\,\dfrac{z}{w(w - z)}$. Its poles inside $C_N$ are at $w = z$ (residue $\pi\cot\pi z$), at $w = n$ for $0 < |n| \le N$ (residue $\dfrac{z}{n(n - z)}$, since $\pi\cot\pi w$ has residue $1$ there), and a double pole at $w = 0$. Near $0$, $\pi\cot\pi w = \frac1w + O(w)$, so the residue there is that of $\frac{z}{w^2(w - z)}$, namely $\frac{d}{dw}\frac{z}{w - z}\big|_{w=0} = -\frac1z$. On $C_N$, $|k(w)| \le \dfrac{2\pi|z|}{(N + \frac12)(N + \frac12 - |z|)}$ and the length of $C_N$ is $8(N + \tfrac12)$, so $\oint_{C_N}k \to 0$. By the residue theorem,

$$\pi\cot\pi z - \frac1z + \sum_{0<|n|\le N}\frac{z}{n(n-z)} \to 0.$$

Pairing $n$ with $-n$: $\frac{z}{n(n-z)} + \frac{z}{n(n+z)} = \frac{2z}{n^2 - z^2}$. This gives the cotangent formula.

Step 2: from cotangent to sine. Let $P(z) = \pi z\prod_{n\ge1}(1 - z^2/n^2)$; by the previous section $P$ is entire with simple zeros exactly at the integers, and for $z \notin \mathbb{Z}$ its logarithmic derivative is $$\frac{P'}{P} = \frac1z + \sum\frac{-2z/n^2}{1 - z^2/n^2} = \frac1z + \sum\frac{2z}{z^2 - n^2} = \pi\cot\pi z$$. Hence $\big(P/\sin\pi z\big)' = \frac{P}{\sin\pi z}\big(\frac{P'}{P} - \pi\cot\pi z\big) = 0$ on the connected set $\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$, so $P = c\sin\pi z$. As $z \to 0$, $P(z)/(\pi z) \to 1$ and $\sin(\pi z)/(\pi z) \to 1$, so $c = 1$.

blocks.title: Weierstrass and Hadamard: products for every entire function
blocks.body:
To build an entire function with prescribed zeros $a_1, a_2, \ldots \to \infty$ in general, Weierstrass introduced the elementary factors

$$E_0(z) = 1 - z, \qquad E_k(z) = (1 - z)\exp\Big(z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \cdots + \frac{z^k}{k}\Big).$$

The exponential cancels the first $k$ terms of $\log(1 - z) = -z - z^2/2 - \cdots$, so $|1 - E_k(z)| \le |z|^{k+1}$ for $|z| \le 1$, and $\prod E_k(z/a_n)$ converges whenever $\sum|a_n|^{-(k+1)} < \infty$; taking $k = n$ for the $n$-th factor always works.

Weierstrass factorisation theorem (stated without proof). Every entire $f \not\equiv 0$ with a zero of order $m$ at $0$ and other zeros $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ (with multiplicity) can be written $f(z) = e^{g(z)}z^m\prod_n E_n(z/a_n)$ with $g$ entire. Conversely, for any sequence $a_n \to \infty$ such a product is an entire function with exactly those zeros.

Hadamard factorisation theorem (stated without proof). If $f$ has finite order $\rho$ and $k = \lfloor\rho\rfloor$, then

$$f(z) = e^{P(z)}z^m\prod_n E_k(z/a_n),$$

with $P$ a polynomial of degree at most $k$. Moreover $\sum_n|a_n|^{-s} < \infty$ for every $s > \rho$, so functions of small order have few zeros. The proof rests on Jensen's formula, $$\log|f(0)| = \sum_{|a_n| < R}\log\frac{|a_n|}{R} + \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\log|f(Re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta$$ (for $f(0) \ne 0$ and no zeros on $|z| = R$), which converts a bound on growth into a bound on the number of zeros in a disc. For the sine, $\rho = 1$ and $k = 1$; pairing $E_1(z/n)E_1(-z/n) = 1 - z^2/n^2$ recovers Euler's product with $P = \log\pi$.

blocks.title: Euler's sums from the product
blocks.body: Use the sine product to evaluate $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^2$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^4$.
blocks.solution:
Compare Taylor coefficients at $z = 0$. On one side,

$$\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z} = 1 - \frac{\pi^2}{6}z^2 + \frac{\pi^4}{120}z^4 - \cdots.$$

On the other, expanding $\prod(1 - z^2/n^2)$ (legitimate, since the product converges uniformly near $0$ and we may compare coefficients of holomorphic functions), the coefficient of $z^2$ is $-\sum 1/n^2$ and that of $z^4$ is $e_2 = \sum_{m<n}\frac{1}{m^2n^2}$. Hence $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$ and $e_2 = \pi^4/120$. Since $\big(\sum 1/n^2\big)^2 = \sum 1/n^4 + 2e_2$,

$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^4} = \frac{\pi^4}{36} - \frac{\pi^4}{60} = \frac{\pi^4}{90}.$$

Continuing in the same way gives $\zeta(2k)$ as a rational multiple of $\pi^{2k}$ for every $k$ (see [[zeta]]).

blocks.title: Wallis's product and the cosine
blocks.body: Deduce Wallis's product $\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \prod_{n\ge1}\dfrac{4n^2}{4n^2 - 1} = \dfrac{2\cdot2}{1\cdot3}\cdot\dfrac{4\cdot4}{3\cdot5}\cdot\dfrac{6\cdot6}{5\cdot7}\cdots$, and the product formula $\cos\pi z = \prod_{n \text{ odd}}\big(1 - 4z^2/n^2\big)$.
blocks.solution:
Put $z = 1/2$ in the sine product: $1 = \frac{\pi}{2}\prod_{n\ge1}\Big(1 - \frac{1}{4n^2}\Big) = \frac\pi2\prod\frac{4n^2 - 1}{4n^2}$, and take reciprocals. Convergence is slow: the partial product up to $n = 1000$ is about $1.5704$ against $\pi/2 \approx 1.5708$.

For the cosine, apply the sine product to $\sin 2\pi z = 2\pi z\prod_{n\ge1}(1 - 4z^2/n^2)$ and split the factors into even $n = 2m$, which give $\prod_m(1 - z^2/m^2)$, and odd $n$. (Rearranging is allowed because $\sum 4|z|^2/n^2$ converges, so the product converges absolutely.) Thus $\sin 2\pi z = 2\sin\pi z\prod_{n\text{ odd}}(1 - 4z^2/n^2)$, and comparing with $\sin 2\pi z = 2\sin\pi z\cos\pi z$ gives the cosine product for $z \notin \mathbb{Z}$, hence for all $z$ by continuity.

blocks.title: Growth determines the function
blocks.body: (a) Find all entire functions with $|f(z)| \le 3 + |z|^{3/2}$ for all $z$. (b) Find all entire $f$ with $|f(z)| \le e^{\operatorname{Re}z}$ for all $z$. (c) Show that an entire function of order less than $1$ with no zeros is constant.
blocks.solution:
(a) $3 + |z|^{3/2} \le 3(1 + |z|)^{3/2}$, so by the polynomial-growth Liouville theorem $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $3/2$, i.e. $f(z) = az + b$ is linear. No non-linear function qualifies, while many linear ones do: for example every $az + b$ with $|a| \le 1$ and $|b| \le 2$, because $|az + b| \le |z| + 2 \le 3 + |z|^{3/2}$ (using $|z| \le 1 + |z|^{3/2}$). Deciding exactly which pairs $(a,b)$ work is then a real-variable exercise.

(b) $g(z) = f(z)e^{-z}$ is entire with $|g(z)| \le e^{\operatorname{Re}z}e^{-\operatorname{Re}z} = 1$, so $g$ is a constant $c$ with $|c| \le 1$. Answer: $f(z) = ce^z$ with $|c| \le 1$.

(c) By Hadamard with $\rho < 1$, $k = 0$ and there are no zeros, so $f = e^{P}$ with $\deg P \le 0$: constant. (Without Hadamard: $f = e^g$ for an entire $g$, and the growth bound forces $\operatorname{Re}g(z) \le B|z|^\rho + \log A$; a Borel–Carathéodory estimate then makes $g$ a polynomial of degree $\le \rho < 1$.) The function $e^z$ shows that order $1$ is the threshold.

blocks.body:
- Zeros do not determine an entire function: $\sin\pi z$ and $e^{z^2}\sin\pi z$ have the same zeros. The factor $e^{g}$ is unavoidable, and finite order is what makes $g$ a polynomial.
- A product whose partial products tend to $0$ without any factor vanishing does not count as convergent. For example, $\prod_{n\ge2}\big(1 + (-1)^n/\sqrt n\big)$ has partial products tending to $0$ (roughly like $N^{-1/2}$), even though $\sum(-1)^n/\sqrt n$ converges: the criterion needs $\sum|a_n| < \infty$, or at least convergence of $\sum\log(1+a_n)$.
- $\prod(1 - z/n)$ diverges; only the symmetric pairing or convergence factors $e^{z/n}$ make the sine product work.
- Order is about growth in all directions at once: $e^z$ is bounded on the left half-plane and on the imaginary axis, but still has order $1$.
- Liouville's theorem needs $f$ holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$; $1/(1 + z^2)$ tends to $0$ at infinity but is not entire.

Entire functions are where the theory of [[holomorphic]] functions meets growth, and their products are built and verified with [[residues]]. Hadamard's theorem is used for the [[gamma]] function, $1/\Gamma(z) = ze^{\gamma z}\prod(1 + z/n)e^{-z/n}$, which with the sine product gives the reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z) = \pi/\sin\pi z$. Applied to the completed zeta function $\xi(s)$, of order $1$, it gives a product over the [[nontrivial-zeros]] of [[zeta]], which is the starting point of the [[explicit-formula]] and of the classical proof of the [[pnt|prime number theorem]] with error term. Jensen's formula is the basic tool for counting zeros, and growth plus zeros is a recurring theme in [[l-functions]] and [[functional-equation]] arguments.

1. Show that $\cos\sqrt z$ is entire of order $1/2$ and find its zeros. Check that $\sum|a_n|^{-s}$ converges exactly for $s > 1/2$.
2. Prove that the product $\prod_{n\ge2}\big(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\big)$ converges and equals $\frac12$ by telescoping.
3. Take the logarithmic derivative of the cosine product to obtain an expansion of $\pi\tan\pi z$ as a sum over odd integers.
4. Show that if $f$ is entire and $\operatorname{Re}f(z) \le 0$ for all $z$, then $f$ is constant. (Hint: consider $e^{f}$.)
